questions.prompt: An impedance \(Z_F\) connects the input and output of an ideal amplifier with gain \(A\). Seen from the input, what is it equivalent to?
options: An impedance \(Z_F(1 - A)\) from the input to ground
An impedance \(Z_F/(1 - A)\) from the input to ground
An impedance \(Z_F\) from the input to ground
An impedance \(AZ_F\) in series with the input
questions.explanation: The current is \(i_{in} = (v_{in} - Av_{in})/Z_F = v_{in}/[Z_F/(1 - A)]\) (reader Eqs. 14.20 to 14.23). For negative \(A\) the impedance shrinks.

questions.prompt: Physically, why does an inverting gain multiply a bridging capacitor?
options: The amplifier adds charge to the capacitor's plates
The capacitor's dielectric constant rises with gain
The voltage across the capacitor is \((1 - A)\) times the input swing, so it draws that much more current
The output resistance appears in series with it
questions.explanation: Capacitor current follows the rate of change of the voltage across it; the far terminal moves \(|A|\) times as much in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Solve the same stage exactly (two nodes, no load capacitance). What is the true \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency in MHz?
questions.explanation: The exact \(b_1\) adds \(R_oC_{gd} = 0.02\ \mathrm{ns}\) to the Miller time constant of 1.98 ns (Eq. 14.30), and the second pole is far away, so the exact answer, 79.7 MHz, lands within a few percent of the 80.4 MHz Miller estimate.

questions.prompt: You double \(R_D\) of a CS stage to double its gain. What happens to the Miller input pole when \(g_mR_o \gg 1\)?
options: It doubles
It does not change
It moves to the right half plane
It roughly halves, because \(C_M\) roughly doubles
questions.explanation: \(C_M \approx g_mR_oC_{gd}\) grows with the gain: the CS stage trades bandwidth for gain at its input.

questions.explanation: Total input capacitance must stay below \(1/(2\pi\cdot10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\cdot100\ \mathrm{MHz}) = 159.2\ \mathrm{fF}\). So \((1 + |A|)\cdot5 \le 139.2\), \(|A| \le 26.8\).

questions.prompt: Why is the Miller result only an estimate?
options: It uses the low-frequency gain, although \(Z_F\) itself changes the gain at high frequency
Because Miller's theorem is algebraically wrong
Because it ignores \(C_{gs}\)
Because it only holds for resistors
questions.explanation: The theorem is exact for the true \(A\), but that \(A\) depends on the bridging capacitor. Taking \(A \approx -g_mR_o\) drops the zero and the output-pole interaction.

Its effective input capacitance nearly vanishes, \(C_{gs}(1 - A) \approx 0\)
It doubles
It becomes negative and large
questions.explanation: A bridging capacitor whose two ends move together carries almost no current: it is bootstrapped.
